strategy: Timeline (today 3 Oct 2026 to about 14 Feb 2027, ~19 weeks): Oct-Nov = finish first-pass learning; Dec = PYQs and subject tests plus first revision; Jan = full-length mocks and second revision; Feb = light revision only.

Oct 2026: finish or strengthen the maths core (Probability & Statistics, Linear Algebra, Calculus & Optimization, ~28-43 marks/yr) and PDSA in Python (16-21 marks/yr). Do 1 GA PYQ set (10 Q, 30 min) every 2-3 days throughout.

Nov 2026: Machine Learning (rising: 11 -> 14 -> 16) and DBMS & Warehousing (18 marks in 2026: B+ trees, SQL, relational algebra, normalization), then AI (search, logic, Bayes-net exact/approximate inference) by early December.
Make the 7 subjects plus GA the tracker's unit of work. Weight hours by the 3-year average marks: PDSA ~18, P&S ~15, ML ~14, DBMS ~12, LA ~12, AI ~7, Calculus ~8, GA 15.
Revise in spaced cycles: revisit each finished topic after ~1 week, ~15 days and ~1 month (GO Classes' 'every 15 days' rule). Keep a one-page formula/insight sheet and a mistake log per subject.

Use PYQs in two passes: (1) topic-wise right after finishing each topic (GATE Overflow tags gate-ds-ai-2024, gateda-2025, gateda-2026, plus related GATE CSE PYQs for DS/Algo, DBMS, Probability and LA); (2) the 3 official DA papers as timed full-length mocks in Dec-Jan, analysed line by line.
Mock cadence: 1 subject or topic test per week from Oct; 1 full-length mock per week from mid-Dec; 2-3 per week from mid-Jan to early Feb. Spend at least as long analysing each mock as taking it.
Free mocks to use: NPTEL-GATE Sunday mocks, GO Classes free AIMTs (Dec-Jan), Piyush Wairale's free DA mocks; add one paid series (GO Classes / Piyush Wairale / MADE EASY) if budget allows.

Exam technique: attempt GA first (about 20 min, target 12-15 marks), then 1-markers, then 2-markers. MSQ and NAT have no negative marking, so never leave them blank. Skip MCQs where you can't eliminate at least 2 options (-1/3 or -2/3). Practise with the GATE virtual calculator.
Code tracing is a large part of the paper: practise reading Python snippets (recursion, list/dict mutation, sorting passes, swap counts, tree traversals) on paper, without running them.

Final 2 weeks: no new topics. Re-read formula sheets and mistake logs, re-solve wrong PYQs and mock questions, and do 2 full mocks in the real 2:30-5:30 PM slot to set your body clock (DA has been an afternoon paper).

Admin: complete the application (extended deadline 12 Oct 2026, correction window 14-21 Oct), check the paper-wise schedule (Dec/Jan) and city allotment (4 Jan 2027), and download the admit card as soon as it is released.

nodes.title: Probability & Statistics
nodes.summary: The single biggest maths block in GATE DA: expect NAT-heavy questions on conditional probability/Bayes, expectation & variance, named distributions (normal, exponential, uniform, Poisson, binomial), conditional expectation from joint PDFs, plus a few inferential-stats questions (CLT, confidence intervals, z/t/chi-squared tests). Speed with standard results (memoryless property, E/Var tables, standard-normal symmetry) decides marks.
nodes.notesGuide: 1) Download the MIT 18.05 (Spring 2022) class reading PDFs from the 'Classes, Reading and In-Class Materials' page: Class 1b, 2, 3, 4a, 4b, 5a–5d, 6a, 6b, 7a, 7b, 17b, 18, 19, 22 cover essentially the whole GATE DA syllabus — print these, they are short (5–15 pages each) and exam-aligned. 2) Keep the free Blitzstein & Hwang 'Introduction to Probability' PDF (probabilitybook.net) as the reference book for harder problems (Ch 1–7, 9, 10). 3) For inferential statistics (CI, z/t/chi-squared tests, sampling distributions) use OpenIntro Statistics (free PDF) Ch 5–7 or NPTEL Somesh Kumar weeks 8–12. 4) Make your own short notes as a 2–3 page formula sheet: one table of every distribution (PMF/PDF, CDF, mean, variance, MGF-free key property such as memorylessness), one page of identities (total probability, Bayes, law of total expectation/variance, Var(aX+bY), Cov/Corr properties), and one page of test-selection rules (z vs t vs chi-squared, df, one/two-tailed, CI formulas). 5) While solving PYQs on GATE Overflow, log every trap you fall into (e.g. confusing independence with mutual exclusion, mean vs rate parametrisation of exponential) in an 'error log' at the end of the notes and revise it weekly.

nodes.title: Linear Algebra
nodes.summary: The highest-yield maths area in GATE DA: expect 4–6 questions (many MSQ/NAT) on rank/nullity, eigenvalues, projection/rank-1 matrices (uu^T, I - 11^T/n) and singular values. Questions reward structural insight (eigenvalues of special matrices, rank arguments) far more than heavy computation.
nodes.notesGuide: 1) Download the free 'Mathematics for Machine Learning' PDF (mml-book.github.io/book/mml-book.pdf) and print Ch 2 (Linear Algebra), Ch 3 (Analytic Geometry: projections, orthogonality) and Ch 4 (Matrix Decompositions: det, eigen, Cholesky, SVD) - this matches the DA syllabus almost exactly. 2) Follow MIT 18.06 lectures and download the per-lecture summary + problem-set PDFs from the 18.06SC session pages (each session has a lecture summary, problems and solutions). 3) Keep Strang's free ILA 6th-edition chapter solutions (math.mit.edu/~gs/linearalgebra/ila6/ chXXasols.pdf) and SVD_Slides.pdf for revision. 4) Use Uday Khankhoje's IIT Madras EE5120 web notes (ee.iitm.ac.in/~uday/notes/linalg/) as a compact second reading. 5) Make your own 4–5 page 'formula + trap' sheet: rank-nullity, rank(AB)<=min, rank(A^TA)=rank(A), trace=sum eig, det=product eig, eigenvalues of A^k, A^-1, A+cI, uu^T (eigs: ||u||^2,0,...), projection P=A(A^TA)^-1A^T (P^2=P, P^T=P, eig 0/1), orthogonal Q (|eig|=1, det ±1), idempotent (rank=trace), block-matrix det/inverse rules, quadratic form definiteness tests, SVD (singular values = sqrt eig of A^TA). Add every PYQ you get wrong as a one-line trap to this sheet.
nodes.tips: Past-paper weightage: GfG 2024 (6 Q), GfG 2025 (11 Q), Piyush Wairale 2026 (2x1 + 3x2). Varies a lot from year to year.

Add each PYQ trap.

nodes.title: Programming, DS & Algorithms
nodes.summary: High-yield, mostly tracing-based section: predict the output of Python snippets (recursion, closures, mutable defaults, list aliasing), simulate sorts/searches/traversals, and reason about simple complexity. Depth is modest but accuracy on code tracing decides the marks.
nodes.notesGuide: 1) Base course: NPTEL 'Programming, DS & Algorithms using Python' (nptel.ac.in/courses/106106145) - download the lecture slides/transcripts from the course page and keep one page of notes per week. 2) Download MIT 6.006 Spring 2020 lecture-note PDFs (OCW 'Lecture Notes' page) for sorting, hashing, BFS/DFS and Dijkstra, and Open Data Structures (ods-python.pdf) chapters 2-3 (array/linked structures), 5 (hashing), 6 (BSTs), 12 (graphs). 3) For Python, build a 'traps sheet' from the official docs: mutable default args (Tutorial 4.8.1), closures/scoping (Execution Model), list aliasing vs copy, slicing with negative steps, integer vs float division, dict/set ordering, string immutability - write each trap as a 3-line snippet + output. 4) Make a one-page 'algorithm card' table: for each search/sort - best/avg/worst time, space, stable?, in-place?, #swaps/#comparisons pattern, behaviour on sorted/reverse input. 5) Hand-trace every DA PYQ snippet on paper first, then confirm on pythontutor.com; log mistakes in an error notebook and revise it weekly.
nodes.tips: Past-paper weightage: GfG 2024 (13 Q), GfG 2025 (10 Q), Piyush Wairale 2026 (4x1 + 6x2). Consistently one of the top two subjects; mostly Python code tracing.

nodes.notesGuide: 1) Core DBMS: download the db-book.com 7th-edition slide PDFs ch2 (relational model), ch3-4 (SQL, integrity constraints, data types), ch6 (ER), ch7 (normalization), ch13 (file organization), ch14 (indexing), ch27 (relational algebra & tuple calculus) and annotate them while watching Gate Smashers or NPTEL IIT-KGP lectures. 2) Keep CMU 15-445 lecture-note PDFs 01, 02, 05 (compression), 08-09 (B+ trees) as crisp secondary notes. 3) Warehousing/preprocessing: download Han-Kamber-Pei slides 03Preprocessing.ppt and 04OLAP.ppt from hanj.cs.illinois.edu and db-book ch11 (Data Analytics); condense into a 2-page sheet of formulas (min-max, z-score, decimal scaling, equal-width/equal-frequency binning, sampling types) and schema diagrams (star, snowflake, fact constellation), plus the distributive/algebraic/holistic measures table. 4) Make your own one-page cheat sheets: RA operator -> SQL equivalent; SQL NULL/aggregate/duplicate rules; closure/candidate-key algorithm + 1NF->BCNF test checklist + lossless/dependency-preserving tests; B/B+ tree order & fan-out formulas. 5) Practise SQL hands-on (SQLBolt, pgexercises) and evaluate every PYQ query on its sample tables by hand, recording mistakes in an error log.

nodes.title: Machine Learning
nodes.summary: The largest technical section of GATE DA: expect numerical questions on regression (OLS/ridge), logistic/naive Bayes/kNN computations, SVM margins, decision-tree entropy/information gain, k-means/hierarchical clustering traces and PCA eigen-computations, plus conceptual MCQ/MSQ on bias-variance, cross-validation and neural networks.
nodes.notesGuide: 1) Download the free ISLP PDF (statlearning.com -> ISLP download page) and use it as the primary text: Ch 3 (linear regression), Ch 4 (logistic, LDA, naive Bayes, kNN), Ch 5 (LOOCV/k-fold), Ch 6.2 (ridge), Ch 8 (trees), Ch 9 (SVM), Ch 10 (neural nets), Ch 12 (PCA, k-means, hierarchical). 2) Download Stanford CS229 main_notes.pdf for the math layer (normal equations, logistic MLE, GDA vs naive Bayes, SVM dual, backprop, bias-variance). Keep Bishop PRML (free Microsoft PDF) only as a reference for LDA (Ch 4) and PCA (Ch 12). 3) For quick 1-page reads per algorithm, the Cornell CS4780 (Kilian Weinberger) HTML lecture notes are excellent - print/save kNN, naive Bayes, logistic, linear regression, SVM, bias-variance, decision trees, neural nets notes. 4) Make your own short notes as one A4 sheet per algorithm with fixed headings: model/hypothesis, loss/objective, closed form or update rule, key hyperparameters, effect of hyperparameters on bias/variance, a tiny hand-worked numeric example (e.g. 4-point k-means, 3-point OLS, entropy of a 2-class split), and 'GATE traps'. 5) Maintain a separate formula sheet: OLS beta=(X^T X)^-1 X^T y, ridge (X^T X+lambda I)^-1 X^T y, sigmoid/log-odds, entropy & information gain & Gini, SVM margin 2/||w||, LOOCV formula for linear smoothers, PCA = eigenvectors of covariance, variance explained ratios, linkage definitions. 6) After each topic, solve the matching GATE Overflow tag page questions and add every mistake to an 'error log' section at the bottom of that topic's sheet. Watch the StatQuest video first if a concept doesn't click, then return to ISLP.

nodes.title: Artificial Intelligence
nodes.summary: Highly scorable, algorithm-tracing section: expect BFS/DFS/UCS/A* node-expansion order and heuristic admissibility/consistency, minimax values and alpha-beta pruned nodes, propositional/first-order logic validity and translations, and Bayesian-network questions on conditional independence, variable elimination and sampling.
nodes.notesGuide: 1) Use the free Berkeley CS188 online textbook (inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/textbook) as the main notes - read Search (state spaces, uninformed, informed), Games (minimax), Logic (propositional, FOL, inference) and Bayes Nets (representation, d-separation, elimination, approximate) sections; these map exactly to the syllabus. 2) Keep AIMA's free pseudocode PDF (aima.cs.berkeley.edu/algorithms.pdf) for exact algorithm definitions (graph vs tree search, alpha-beta, resolution, enumeration, rejection/likelihood weighting). 3) Watch MIT 6.034 Lectures 4-6 (search & games) and 21-22 (probabilistic inference) and the NPTEL Mausam course for depth. 4) Make short notes as tables: for each search algorithm -> fringe data structure, complete?, optimal?, time/space, tie-breaking convention; for heuristics -> admissible/consistent definitions + dominance; for games -> alpha/beta update rules and pruning condition with one fully worked tree. 5) For logic, keep a 1-page sheet of equivalences (De Morgan, implication, contrapositive), CNF conversion, resolution, quantifier negation and common English->FOL patterns; reuse your Discrete Maths logic notes. 6) For Bayes nets, write the factorization rule, the three d-separation triples (causal chain, common cause, common effect) and a worked variable-elimination example, plus prior/rejection/likelihood-weighting/Gibbs sampling steps. 7) Practise with CS188 Fall 2024 exam-prep worksheets (with solutions), then GATE DA PYQs and the old GATE CSE AI questions on GATE Overflow.
nodes.tips: Past-paper weightage: GfG 2024 (7 Q), GfG 2025 (2 Q), Piyush Wairale 2026 (4x1 + 2x2). Unpredictable, but search and Bayes-net inference come up repeatedly.

nodes.title: General Aptitude
nodes.summary: Common section in every GATE paper: 10 questions (5 x 1-mark + 5 x 2-mark) = 15 marks, MCQ/MSQ/NAT, 1/3 or 2/3 negative marking on wrong MCQs only. The GATE 2027 GA syllabus (IIT Madras) has four sections: Verbal Aptitude (grammar, vocabulary, reading comprehension, narrative sequencing), Quantitative Aptitude (data interpretation, numerical computation & estimation, mensuration & geometry, elementary statistics & probability), Analytical Aptitude (deduction/induction, analogy, numerical relations & reasoning) and Spatial Aptitude (translation, rotation, scaling, mirroring, assembling, grouping, paper folding/cutting, 2D/3D patterns). Questions are school-level but tricky; toppers score 12-15/15. Best ROI: ~40-60 hours spread over the prep period, mostly solving PYQs from all GATE branches (GA questions are identical in style across papers, so 100+ sets of PYQs exist).
nodes.notesGuide: Keep ONE slim GA notebook (or a single digital doc) with 4 tabs = the 4 syllabus sections. (1) Quant: a one-page formula sheet per topic (percent/ratio shortcuts, log & exponent rules, nPr/nCr + circular/identical-object cases, AP/GP sums, areas/volumes/surface areas, triangle & circle theorems, mean/median/mode/SD, basic probability rules) - write each formula with ONE worked PYQ beside it. (2) Verbal: a running 'error log' of grammar rules you got wrong (article/preposition/tense/subject-verb agreement) with the exact sentence, plus a vocabulary list of words/idioms from GATE PYQs (word, meaning, the PYQ sentence). (3) Analytical: a 'pattern bank' - for each PYQ type (syllogism/deduction, seating/arrangement, analogy, number relations) write the solving template in 3-5 steps and draw the diagram/table you used. (4) Spatial: sketch every paper-folding/cutting, cube-net, mirror/rotation PYQ by hand with the answer figure - redrawing builds the visual skill. Maintain a 'mistake log' table (date, source/PYQ id, topic, why wrong: concept/calculation/misread, fix) and revisit it weekly. Before each mock, re-read only the formula sheet + mistake log (15 min).
nodes.tips: Past-paper weightage: Fixed by the exam pattern: 10 Q (5x1 + 5x2).

children.title: Verbal Aptitude
children.tips: Usually 2-3 one-mark questions per paper - near-guaranteed marks. Read the whole sentence, identify the grammatical slot (tense/article/preposition) before reading options. Keep a PYQ vocabulary list; GATE reuses word families. Don't overthink: pick the most natural, formal English. GATE RC passages are 4-8 lines; answers are 'what can be inferred' - choose the option that is strictly supported, never the one that is merely true in the real world. For sequencing, find the opening sentence (introduces a noun) and pronoun/connector links (however, this, thus) to chain sentences.

children.title: Quantitative Aptitude
children.tips: Largest share of GA marks. Memorise percent-fraction equivalents (1/8 = 12.5%, etc.), successive change formula a+b+ab/100, log rules, and nCr identities. Many are NAT - compute carefully and re-check units. For P&C, decide first: order matters? repetition allowed? identical objects? circular? Typically one 2-mark question. Read axis labels/units and the exact question (percentage of what?). Approximate first, then compute only if options are close. Practice with a timer: 3 minutes per DI question. Recent DA papers (2025, 2026) had shaded-area circle questions. Draw the figure, mark all known lengths/angles, decompose into standard shapes. Memorise sector area = (theta/360)*pi*r^2 and inscribed-angle theorem. Low effort for DA aspirants - fully covered by your Probability & Statistics subject. Just practice GA-style wording and do 20-30 PYQs.
